title: Critical Science Plan for the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST)
extended_summary:
This paper presents the Critical Science Plan for the Daniel K. Inouye Solar Telescope (DKIST), outlining the major solar-physics questions the telescope is expected to address as it nears start of operations. Rather than reporting an empirical study, it synthesizes the priorities of the DKIST Science Working Group and community contributors to identify the science that DKIST’s unique aperture, wavelength coverage, spatial resolution, polarimetric sensitivity, and adaptive optics will enable.

The plan focuses on four broad research areas: magnetoconvection and dynamo processes, flares and eruptive activity, magnetic connectivity through the non-eruptive solar atmosphere, and long-term studies of the Sun and broader implications. Across these areas, the paper argues that DKIST will allow new measurements of small-scale photospheric magnetic fields, wave excitation and propagation, solar irradiance modulation, sunspot structure and formation, flare precursors, coronal magnetic fields, and energy transport through the solar atmosphere. It emphasizes the importance of combining DKIST observations with numerical simulations and other observatories.

The context is the solar atmosphere, not an educational setting. The paper’s main conclusion is that DKIST’s unprecedented observational capabilities will make it possible to resolve long-standing questions in solar and stellar magnetism, and that the telescope will be especially valuable for studies requiring high-resolution spectropolarimetry across multiple atmospheric heights. No participant population, intervention study, or learning outcome data are reported.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a solar physics critical science plan, not an educational intervention study. It does not evaluate Khanmigo or any K-12 learning technology, and it reports no empirical education methodology or learner outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact is reported or inferable for K-12 science learning. The paper is purely a scientific roadmap for DKIST capabilities and contains no evidence about student learning, implementation, or classroom use.
